content.title: About
content.content: Nature Valley Crunchy Granola Bar is a crunchy snack made from whole grain oats, nuts, and honey, produced by General Mills. It is designed for quick energy and is popular among hikers and gym‑goers.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first Nature Valley bar was launched in 1975.
Each bar consists of two halves joined by a light crumb that creates the signature crunch.
Common ingredients include sunflower oil, honey, and soy lecithin.
The product is sold in more than 30 countries worldwide.
In Russia, the bars are often found in the health‑food aisle.

items.title: Source of whole grains
items.content: Whole‑grain oats provide slowly digestible carbohydrates and fiber, helping maintain steady energy levels.

items.title: Contains nuts
items.content: Nuts contribute heart‑healthy monounsaturated fats, vitamin E, and magnesium.

items.title: Honey sweetener
items.content: Honey adds a touch of natural sweetness and antioxidants without refined sugar.

items.title: Satiety support
items.content: Fiber and protein help keep you feeling full between meals.

items.title: Convenient snack
items.content: The bar is portable, encouraging healthier snack choices on the go.

items.title: Nut and soy allergy
items.content: The bar may contain peanuts, almonds, or soy lecithin, which can trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Although sweetened with honey, the bar still contains a notable amount of simple sugars.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: One bar (≈42 g) provides about 190–210 kcal, so portion control is advisable.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Some varieties include added salt, which may be a concern for people with hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the bar whole as a quick snack, crumble it into yogurt or oatmeal, or use it as an energy boost before a workout.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place with the package tightly sealed. For extended shelf life, keep in the refrigerator to prevent fat oxidation.

content.title: About
content.content: Crab is a seafood product that comes from marine crustaceans of the family Portunidae and related groups. It lives in coastal waters of temperate and tropical regions. Crab meat is tender, slightly sweet, and has a distinct oceanic aroma. It is eaten raw (e.g., in sushi), boiled, baked, or as canned meat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Crabs can walk sideways thanks to the unique articulation of their legs.
Some crab species can change color to blend with their surroundings.
Crabs have powerful claws used for defense and for catching food.
The largest species, the Japanese spider crab (Macrocheira kaempferi), can have a leg span of up to 3.7 m.
Crabs play an important ecological role by cleaning the sea floor of dead organisms.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Crab meat provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with many other seafoods, crab is low in fat, making it suitable for low‑calorie diets.

items.title: Source of vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 supports nervous system function and red blood cell formation.

items.title: Contains essential minerals
items.content: Crab is a good source of zinc, copper, selenium, and phosphorus, which aid immunity and metabolism.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Crab meat contains polyunsaturated fatty acids that promote heart health.

items.title: Shellfish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience severe allergic reactions to crab.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Crab contains cholesterol, so people with high cholesterol should consume it in moderation.

items.title: Heavy metal contamination
items.content: Crabs from polluted waters can accumulate mercury and cadmium; purchase from reputable sources.

items.title: Purine content
items.content: Crab is high in purines, which may exacerbate gout symptoms.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Crab meat can be used in salads, soups, pastas, rolls, and sushi. It is often boiled, steamed, or baked. Canned crab is convenient for quick dishes. Before eating, the meat should be thoroughly rinsed and the shell removed.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh crab should be kept in the refrigerator at 0–2 °C and used within 2 days. Frozen crab can be stored at –18 °C for up to 6 months. Canned crab is shelf‑stable until the expiration date.

content.title: About
content.content: Cooked garlic consists of peeled garlic cloves that have been boiled until tender. Heat softens the sharp aroma, giving the cloves a mild, slightly sweet flavor and a creamy texture. It is commonly used as a side dish, in sauces, soups, and purees.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cooked garlic is easier on the digestive system than raw garlic.
Thermal processing reduces allicin, the compound responsible for the pungent smell.
In many cuisines, cooked garlic is blended into a paste with olive oil and herbs.
Garlic belongs to the Liliaceae family and is a close relative of onion, leek, and shallot.
Cooked garlic can be kept in the refrigerator for up to a week and frozen for several months.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Garlic contains sulfur compounds such as diallyl disulfide that may enhance the body’s immune defenses.

items.title: Blood pressure reduction
items.content: Studies suggest regular garlic consumption can contribute to modest reductions in blood pressure.

items.title: Antioxidant effect
items.content: Cooked garlic retains vitamin C and selenium, which help combat oxidative stress.

items.title: Cardiovascular health
items.content: Garlic sulfides may improve lipid profiles by lowering LDL cholesterol.

items.title: Digestive aid
items.content: The soft texture of cooked garlic is easy to digest and may promote beneficial gut bacteria.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to garlic, ranging from skin rashes to gastrointestinal symptoms.

items.title: Medication interactions
items.content: Garlic can enhance the effects of anticoagulant drugs, so caution is advised for people on blood‑thinners.

items.title: Heartburn and discomfort
items.content: Sensitive people may experience heartburn or gas after large portions of cooked garlic.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cooked garlic can be served as a simple snack, added to purees, sauces, salads, casseroles, and soups. It also works well mashed into a paste with olive oil, lemon, and herbs.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked garlic in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 7 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑sized bags for up to 3 months. Check for off‑odors or texture changes before use and discard any spoiled pieces.

content.title: About
content.content: Chocolate topping (item 5038) is a finely grated or shaved chocolate intended for sprinkling over desserts, ice cream, baked goods, and drinks. It offers a rich cocoa flavor, sweetness, and a pleasant texture, spreads easily and melts quickly when warmed.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chocolate topping is often made from a blend of milk and dark chocolate to achieve a balanced taste.
Shaved chocolate retains more aromatic compounds than fully melted chocolate.
The topping may contain a small amount of emulsifiers that prevent cocoa particles from clumping.
In some countries chocolate topping is used as a separate ingredient in confectionery mixes.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Cocoa solids are rich in flavonoids that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Mood support
items.content: Chocolate stimulates the production of serotonin and endorphins, improving mood.

items.title: Source of magnesium
items.content: Magnesium in chocolate supports muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Provides iron
items.content: Dark chocolate is a good source of iron, beneficial for blood formation.

items.title: Enriched with cocoa butter
items.content: Cocoa butter contains monounsaturated fats that can fit into a balanced diet.

items.title: Cocoa allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chocolate components.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Topping often contains added sugar, so it should be consumed in moderation.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Chocolate topping is calorie‑dense, which can contribute to weight gain if over‑consumed.

items.title: Caffeine content
items.content: Cocoa contains small amounts of caffeine, which may affect sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Sprinkle chocolate topping over ice cream, cakes, cupcakes, pancakes, hot chocolate, yogurt, or fruit salads. It can also be folded into batter for cookies to create chocolate flecks. For even distribution, lightly dust the dish just before serving.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the chocolate topping in an airtight container in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. For long‑term storage, refrigerate it, but allow it to reach room temperature before use to avoid condensation.
